questions.question: A student says, 'A normal distribution is just any bell-shaped curve, so if two datasets look roughly symmetric, they are basically the same normal distribution.' Do you agree? Explain using the roles of mean and variance, and describe how changing each parameter changes the graph.
questions.expected_answer: A strong answer should reject the claim. A normal distribution is specified by two parameters, mean and variance: X ~ N(mu, sigma^2). The mean shifts the center left or right, while the variance controls spread; larger variance makes the curve wider and lower, smaller variance makes it narrower and taller. So two symmetric bell-shaped curves may both be normal, but they need not be the same normal distribution unless both their means and variances match.

full_credit: States that a normal distribution is determined by mean and variance.
Explains that mean changes location/center.
Explains that variance changes spread/height.
Explicitly rejects the idea that all bell-shaped curves are the same normal.
partial_credit: Mentions mean and variance but does not clearly tie them to graph shape.
Says distributions can differ in center or spread but gives only one parameter correctly.
common_mistakes: Confusing variance and standard deviation.
Saying taller means larger mean.
Treating symmetry alone as enough to identify a normal distribution.

follow_ups.question: If two normal distributions have the same mean but different variances, where do their peaks occur relative to each other, and why?
What two numerical values would you need to specify before you could fully identify a normal distribution?

questions.question: Suppose adult reaction times in milliseconds are modeled as X ~ N(250, 40^2). Without plugging in table values, explain how you would compute the probability that a randomly chosen person has a reaction time between 220 and 300 milliseconds, and interpret the result in terms of areas under a curve.
questions.expected_answer: Standardize both endpoints: Z = (X - 250)/40. Then P(220 <= X <= 300) = P((220-250)/40 <= Z <= (300-250)/40) = Phi(1.25) - Phi(-0.75). The student should explain that this is the area under the standard normal curve between the two z-scores, not the height of the density at those points.

full_credit: Uses correct standardization formula.
Sets up probability as difference of two CDF values.
Interprets answer as area/probability, not density height.
partial_credit: Gets one z-score correct but not the other.
Knows to use Phi but does not clearly show interval subtraction.
common_mistakes: Using the PDF instead of the CDF.
Forgetting to subtract the lower-tail probability.
Using variance 40^2 incorrectly as if standard deviation were 1600.

questions.question: A factory measures the diameter of a part, and past data suggest diameters are approximately normal with mean 10 mm and variance 0.04. The quality manager wants the probability a part falls between 9.8 and 10.1 mm. Describe the full modeling and computation steps aloud, including whether you would use variance or standard deviation when standardizing.
questions.expected_answer: First identify that X ~ N(10, 0.04), so the standard deviation is sqrt(0.04) = 0.2. Then standardize: P(9.8 <= X <= 10.1) = P((9.8-10)/0.2 <= Z <= (10.1-10)/0.2) = Phi(0.5) - Phi(-1). A strong answer should stress that standardization uses the standard deviation, not the variance.

full_credit: Correctly identifies sigma = 0.2 from variance 0.04.
Sets up both z-scores correctly.
Uses Phi difference correctly.
Explicitly notes standard deviation is used in standardization.
partial_credit: Correct method with arithmetic slip.
Understands interval probability but is vague about variance vs standard deviation.
common_mistakes: Dividing by 0.04 instead of 0.2.
Confusing variance notation with standard deviation notation.
Using symmetry without computing both endpoints.

questions.question: You are modeling student heights from one classroom. Someone argues that using a normal model is justified because 'this classroom histogram looks nice and smooth,' while another person argues it is useful because the model generalizes through mean and variance. Compare these justifications and say which is stronger.
questions.expected_answer: A strong answer should say that visual fit to one sample can be suggestive, but the stronger justification is that the normal family is a flexible model summarized by mean and variance and often generalizes well across similar contexts. The student can mention that Gaussian models are often used because many real-valued measurements are approximately normal and because a Gaussian is a principled distribution once mean and variance are specified. The answer should distinguish descriptive fit from modeling rationale.

questions.question: Let X1, X2, and X3 be independent Gaussian random variables with means 5, -2, and 1 and variances 4, 9, and 16 respectively. Without deriving from scratch, give the distribution of S = X1 + X2 + X3 and explain why the variance adds the way it does.
questions.expected_answer: Because sums of independent Gaussians are Gaussian, S is normal. Its mean is 5 + (-2) + 1 = 4, and its variance is 4 + 9 + 16 = 29, so S ~ N(4, 29). The variances add because independence makes covariance terms zero.

questions.question: Suppose X ~ N(100, 15^2), and you take an independent sample of size 10. Explain the distribution of the sample mean, and then set up the probability that the sample mean lies between 95 and 105. Do not just state the answer; explain where the new standard deviation comes from.
questions.expected_answer: For i.i.d. normal observations, the sample mean is also normal: Xbar ~ N(100, 15^2/10), equivalently standard deviation 15/sqrt(10). Therefore P(95 <= Xbar <= 105) = Phi((105-100)/(15/sqrt(10))) - Phi((95-100)/(15/sqrt(10))). The reduction in spread comes from averaging independent observations, which divides the variance by n.

questions.question: A classmate says, 'Whenever I see a binomial random variable with large n, I will use a normal approximation.' Give a careful response. Your answer should discuss when a normal approximation is reasonable, when a Poisson approximation is more appropriate, and what independence assumption matters for the normal case.
questions.expected_answer: The statement is too broad. For a binomial Bin(n,p), a normal approximation is good when n is large and p is not too close to 0 or 1; a common rule is np(1-p) > 10, and the trials should be independent. If n is large but p is very small, then Poisson with lambda = np is often better. So 'large n' alone is not sufficient; the value of p and the dependence assumptions matter.

full_credit: Rejects 'large n alone' as sufficient.
States a normal-approximation criterion involving np(1-p).
States a Poisson-approximation regime with large n and small p.
Mentions independence for the normal approximation.
partial_credit: Identifies one approximation regime correctly but not the comparison.
Mentions p near 0 or 1 is problematic but gives no criterion.
common_mistakes: Saying Poisson is always better when n is large.
Ignoring p entirely.
Forgetting continuity correction if using normal for a discrete variable.

follow_ups.question: For Bin(100, 0.04), which approximation would you prefer first, and why?
If p = 0.5 and n = 100, does that look more like a normal-approximation setting or a Poisson-approximation setting?

questions.question: Consider three binomial distributions: Bin(100, 0.5), Bin(100, 0.04), and Bin(100, 0.96). A student claims that Poisson should approximate all three because n is 100 in every case. Evaluate each case separately, and for the third one explain the useful trick if you still want a Poisson-style approximation.
questions.expected_answer: Bin(100,0.5) is not a good Poisson candidate because p is not small and lambda = 50 is not in the sparse-event regime; a normal approximation is more natural. Bin(100,0.04) is a good Poisson candidate with lambda = 4 because n is large and p is small. Bin(100,0.96) is not directly suitable for Poisson on the number of successes, but one can approximate the number of failures, which is Bin(100, 0.04), by Poisson(4), then translate back if needed.

full_credit: Correctly rejects Poisson for Bin(100,0.5).
Correctly accepts Poisson for Bin(100,0.04).
Explains complement/failure-count trick for Bin(100,0.96).

Recognizes that Bin(100,0.96) is problematic but cannot articulate the failure-count trick.
common_mistakes: Using Poisson directly for Bin(100,0.96) successes.
Thinking lambda large automatically helps Poisson approximation.
Not distinguishing rare failures from common successes.

questions.question: Let X ~ Bin(100, 0.5). You want an approximate value for P(48 <= X <= 56) using a normal approximation. Set up the approximation carefully, including the mean, variance, and the continuity correction, and explain why the correction is needed.
questions.expected_answer: For X ~ Bin(100,0.5), the normal approximation is Y ~ N(mu = np = 50, variance = np(1-p) = 25), so standard deviation is 5. Because X is discrete, apply continuity correction: P(48 <= X <= 56) is approximated by P(47.5 < Y < 56.5). Then standardize to get Phi((56.5-50)/5) - Phi((47.5-50)/5). The correction improves the approximation by matching integer masses to intervals on the continuous normal curve.

Uses continuity-corrected bounds 47.5 and 56.5.

questions.question: You are told that the number of floods in a 500-year period is modeled as Poisson with parameter 1. Explain how to compute the probability of at least 3 floods in 500 years, and then describe why summing the lower counts is preferable to summing the infinite upper tail.
questions.expected_answer: If X ~ Poi(1), then P(X >= 3) = 1 - P(X <= 2) = 1 - sum from i=0 to 2 of e^-1 * 1^i / i!. This complement is preferable because the upper tail has infinitely many terms, while the lower tail up to 2 has only three terms. The answer should emphasize the modeling step and the complement trick.

common_mistakes: Using a binomial model with arbitrary n.
Computing P(X=3) instead of P(X>=3).

questions.question: A region is called a '500-year floodplain,' meaning the average flood rate is 1 per 500 years. A student concludes that after 499 years without a flood, a flood is now almost guaranteed next year. Respond to this claim by connecting the counting model and the waiting-time model.
questions.expected_answer: The claim is false. The count of floods over time can be modeled by a Poisson process with rate 1/500 per year, and the waiting time to the next flood is exponential with parameter 1/500. Exponential waiting times are memoryless, so having already waited 499 years does not make next year almost guaranteed; the probability of a flood within the next year is still about 1 - e^(-1/500), approximately 1/500 for small rates.

Connects Poisson counts to exponential waiting time.
Mentions memorylessness or equivalent reasoning.

questions.question: Suppose there are 10 independent floodplains, each with annual flood count modeled as Poisson(1/500). You care about the event that more than 2 of the floodplains have at least 3 floods in a given year. Explain the two-stage modeling strategy and write the final probability expression.
questions.expected_answer: First, for one floodplain let X ~ Poi(1/500) be the number of floods in a year, and compute p* = P(X >= 3) = 1 - sum_{i=0}^2 e^{-1/500}(1/500)^i / i!. Then let Y ~ Bin(10, p*) count how many floodplains satisfy that rare event. The target probability is P(Y > 2) = sum_{i=3}^{10} C(10,i)(p*)^i(1-p*)^{10-i}.

Uses binomial model across 10 independent floodplains.
Writes correct upper-tail binomial sum for more than 2.

Uses p* conceptually but leaves it poorly defined.

questions.question: A botanist thinks a population of rose bushes is actually a mixture of two visually identical species. Species A occurs with probability 2/3 and has flower count approximated by N(4, 4); species B occurs with probability 1/3 and has flower count approximated by N(2, 9). Explain how to compute the probability that a randomly chosen bush has more than 3 flowers, and justify any continuity correction you use.
questions.expected_answer: Condition on species and use the law of total probability. Because flower count is discrete but being approximated by normals, use continuity correction: P(XA > 3) ≈ 1 - Phi((3.5-4)/2), and P(XB > 3) ≈ 1 - Phi((3.5-2)/3). Then combine them: P(X > 3) = (2/3)P(XA > 3) + (1/3)P(XB > 3). The correction is needed because the Gaussian is continuous but the underlying flower count is integer-valued.

Uses continuity correction with threshold 3.5.
Sets up both Gaussian tail probabilities correctly.
Explains why continuity correction is needed.
partial_credit: Gets mixture weighting right but omits continuity correction.
Uses correction conceptually but on only one component.
common_mistakes: Averaging means first and treating mixture as one normal.

questions.question: Using the same two-species rose model, a bush is observed to have exactly 3 flowers. Explain how to compare how likely species B is relative to species A. Do not just say 'use Bayes'; describe why densities appear and how the ratio simplifies.
questions.expected_answer: Because the observation is a single value under continuous approximations, one compares small-interval probabilities around 3, which leads to a ratio of densities. The posterior odds ratio is P(B|X=3) / P(A|X=3) = [f_B(3)P(B)] / [f_A(3)P(A)]. The student should explain that the tiny interval width cancels, so one may use Gaussian PDFs at x=3 multiplied by the priors 1/3 and 2/3.

questions.question: A program first samples X ~ Bernoulli(0.3). If X=0 it returns Y ~ N(-1, 2^2); if X=1 it returns Y ~ N(1, 1^2). Explain how to compute P(Y < 0), and then comment on why treating Y as a single normal with mean equal to the weighted average would be a conceptual mistake.
questions.expected_answer: Condition on the latent Bernoulli variable: P(Y<0) = P(Y<0|X=0)P(X=0) + P(Y<0|X=1)P(X=1) = 0.7 Phi((0-(-1))/2) + 0.3 Phi((0-1)/1). Treating Y as a single normal with the weighted mean would be incorrect because a mixture of normals is generally not itself normal; the shape can be asymmetric or multimodal, and probabilities must be computed from the mixture law.

questions.question: In the same Gaussian-mixture program, suppose the output value observed is y = 0.1. Explain how to compute the posterior probability that the Bernoulli variable was X=1. Your answer should distinguish clearly between probabilities and densities.

Here f_{Y|X=1} is the N(1,1) density and f_{Y|X=0} is the N(-1,4) density, evaluated at 0.1. A strong answer explains that for a continuous observation at a point we use densities because actual point probabilities are zero.

questions.question: An art historian has prior probability 0.75 that a painting is by Van Gogh. A measured feature value is x = 19, and under the two hypotheses the feature is modeled as N(20, 9) if Van Gogh and N(12, 25) otherwise. Explain how to update the belief using Bayes' rule, and say whether you should compare CDF values or PDF values at x = 19.
questions.expected_answer: Use Bayes with likelihoods from the normal densities: P(VG|X=19) = f_VG(19)·0.75 / [f_VG(19)·0.75 + f_not(19)·0.25], where f_VG is the N(20,9) PDF and f_not is the N(12,25) PDF. Since the observation is a specific continuous value, the relevant quantities are densities, not CDFs. The reasoning is that one compares how plausible 19 is under each model and then incorporates the prior odds.

Includes prior 0.75 and complementary prior 0.25.
Explains why densities, not CDFs, are used for an exact observed value.
partial_credit: Gets Bayes structure right but forgets denominator expansion.
Recognizes use of likelihoods but is vague about density vs probability.
common_mistakes: Using Phi-based tail probabilities instead of densities at 19.

questions.question: A random variable X has mean 0.01 and variance 0.482, and you collect 100 independent samples and average them. State the approximate distribution of the average and explain why the variance changes by a factor of 1/100 rather than staying the same.
questions.expected_answer: Let Xbar be the sample average of 100 i.i.d. draws. By the CLT, or exactly if normality held, Xbar is approximately N(0.01, 0.482/100). questions.question: A student approximates X ~ Poi(1000) by N(1000, 1000) and then computes P(990 < X < 1000) using the bounds 990 and 1000 directly. Critique this method carefully. What parts are right, what part needs refinement, and what would the corrected setup look like?
questions.expected_answer: Approximating a large-parameter Poisson by a normal with matching mean and variance is reasonable, so N(1000,1000) is the right approximating distribution. But because the Poisson is discrete and the normal is continuous, continuity correction should be used: P(990 < X < 1000) means X is one of 991 through 999, so the corrected normal approximation is P(990.5 < Y < 999.5) for Y ~ N(1000,1000). Then one standardizes those corrected bounds.

questions.question: Someone says, 'The standard normal is a completely different distribution from the normal distribution.' Give a careful response that includes its parameters, its CDF notation, and why standardization is useful.
questions.expected_answer: The statement is false. The standard normal is just the special case Z ~ N(0,1) of the normal family, with mean 0 and variance 1. Its CDF is denoted Phi(z) = P(Z <= z). Standardization converts a general normal X ~ N(mu, sigma^2) into Z = (X-mu)/sigma, allowing probabilities for any normal to be computed using the single standard normal table or function Phi.

common_mistakes: Calling 1 the standard deviation when asked for variance without clarification.
Saying Phi is the PDF.

questions.question: A factory produces light bulbs, and the lifetime of a single bulb is modeled as a normal random variable with mean 1200 hours and standard deviation 300 hours. An engineer tests 25 bulbs independently and wants the probability that the sample mean lifetime is at least 1300 hours. Explain which random variable you would model, what its distribution is, and how you would express the probability in terms of the standard normal CDF.
questions.expected_answer: Let \(\bar X\) be the sample mean of the 25 independent bulb lifetimes. Because each lifetime is normal, the sample mean is exactly normal: \(\bar X \sim N(1200, 300^2/25)\), so its standard deviation is \(300/5 = 60\). Then the desired probability is \(P(\bar X \ge 1300) = P\left(Z \ge \frac{1300-1200}{60}\right) = 1-\Phi(100/60)\). A strong answer should also note that this is about the mean of a sample, not a single bulb, so the variability is smaller than 300.

questions.question: A student says: 'For any large-count discrete random variable, if I approximate it with a normal distribution, I never need a continuity correction because the normal is already continuous.' Do you agree? Use a concrete example such as approximating a binomial probability like \(P(X \le 50)\) for \(X \sim \text{Bin}(100,0.5)\), and explain what correction should be used and why.
questions.expected_answer: I do not agree. When a normal distribution is used to approximate a discrete random variable, a continuity correction is typically needed because the discrete event places mass on integers, while the normal assigns probability to intervals. For example, if \(X \sim \text{Bin}(100,0.5)\), then \(X\) has mean 50 and variance \(100\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.5 = 25\), so the approximation is \(N(50,25)\). To approximate \(P(X \le 50)\), we use \(P(Y \le 50.5)\), not \(P(Y \le 50)\), where \(Y\sim N(50,25)\). The reason is that the binomial event \(X\le 50\) includes all integer values up through 50, so the corresponding continuous interval should extend halfway past 50.

full_credit: Explicitly disagrees with the claim.
Explains the discrete-versus-continuous mismatch.
Uses a correct continuity correction such as 50.5 for \(P(X\le 50)\), or 49.5 and 50.5 for exact-point events converted to intervals.
Mentions that normal approximation is reasonable here because binomial conditions are met.
partial_credit: Knows a continuity correction is needed but gives the wrong boundary direction.
Explains the idea verbally without a concrete example.
Correctly computes mean and variance but omits why the half-unit adjustment matters.
common_mistakes: Saying continuity correction is only needed for Poisson and not binomial.
Using \(P(Y\le 50)\) directly for \(P(X\le 50)\).
Applying a correction in the wrong direction, such as 49.5 for \(P(X\le 50)\).

questions.question: You are modeling the total score from two independent measurement devices. One device’s error is \(X \sim N(2,4)\), the other’s is \(Y \sim N(-1,9)\), independently. Without doing any integration, explain the distribution of the combined error \(X+Y\), and then explain what assumption would break if the devices were strongly dependent.
questions.expected_answer: Because independent Gaussian random variables add to another Gaussian, \(X+Y\) is normal. Its mean is the sum of the means, \(2+(-1)=1\), and its variance is the sum of the variances, \(4+9=13\), so \(X+Y\sim N(1,13)\). The key assumption is independence; if the device errors were strongly dependent, we could no longer simply add the variances. In that case the variance would be \(\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)=\mathrm{Var}(X)+\mathrm{Var}(Y)+2\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)\), so dependence changes the spread, even though the mean still adds.

Correctly gives mean 1 and variance 13.
Explains that independence justifies adding variances directly.
Identifies covariance as the missing term under dependence.

Uses standard deviations instead of variances when combining spread.
common_mistakes: Adding standard deviations to get 5.

questions.question: A call center tracks the number of successful upsells per day. Historically, each of 400 calls independently leads to an upsell with probability 0.03. A manager proposes two approximations for the distribution of the daily upsell count: Poisson and Normal. Which approximation would you recommend first, which would you avoid, and how would you justify your choice using the problem parameters rather than just intuition?
questions.expected_answer: The exact model is \(X\sim \text{Bin}(400,0.03)\). Since \(n\) is large and \(p\) is small, Poisson is a natural approximation with \(\lambda=np=12\). Normal can also be considered because \(np(1-p)=400\cdot 0.03\cdot 0.97\approx 11.64\), which is above the common threshold of about 10, so the normal conditions are also borderline acceptable. However, based on the guideline 'if there is a choice, use Gaussian to approximate,' I would recommend the normal approximation first, with mean 12 and variance 11.64, and I would remember to use continuity correction for probability calculations. I would avoid saying Poisson is the only valid option; both are defensible here, but the normal is preferred by the stated course heuristic when available.

questions.question: A data scientist builds a classifier using a mixture model. With probability 0.7, a measurement comes from \(N(-1, 2^2)\); with probability 0.3, it comes from \(N(1,1^2)\). You observe a value of 0.1. Explain aloud how to compute the posterior probability that it came from the second component, and why you must use densities rather than probabilities at the single point 0.1.
questions.expected_answer: Let \(C\in\{0,1\}\) indicate the component, with \(P(C=1)=0.3\) and \(P(C=0)=0.7\). Because the observation is continuous, \(P(X=0.1\mid C=i)=0\) for each component, so we use Bayes' rule with densities: \(P(C=1\mid X=0.1)=\frac{f_{1}(0.1)\cdot 0.3}{f_{1}(0.1)\cdot 0.3+f_{0}(0.1)\cdot 0.7}\), where \(f_1\) is the \(N(1,1)\) density and \(f_0\) is the \(N(-1,4)\) density. Concretely, \(f_1(0.1)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac12(0.1-1)^2}\) and \(f_0(0.1)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac12((0.1+1)/2)^2}\). A strong answer should explain that point probabilities are zero for continuous variables, but density ratios still determine the posterior through Bayes' rule.

full_credit: Introduces a latent component variable and states the prior probabilities.
Uses Bayes' rule with densities, not point probabilities.
Writes the posterior as density times prior over total evidence.
Explains why densities are appropriate for a continuous observation at a single point.

Gets the idea of weighting components by likelihood but does not justify the use of densities.
Uses informal proportionality correctly but does not normalize.
common_mistakes: Writing \(P(X=0.1\mid C=i)\) as an ordinary nonzero probability.
Ignoring the prior weights 0.7 and 0.3.
Using CDF values instead of density values for the observed point.
